title: Of Mice and Mentors: Best Laid Plans
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Janetos responds to worry that ELA programs offer excerpts rather than whole books by arguing that shorter complete works, plays and short stories can carry real complexity within a limited school day. She also urges thematic alignment with social studies, noting evidence that extra social studies time is the one subject clearly lifting reading scores. Her wider target is a pattern of overreaction in reading instruction, where schools cross and burn every Science of Reading bridge, overteaching phonics components and chasing programs that are later revised. She proposes asking Carl Hendrick's question of whether a practice improves learning enough to justify its implementation costs, and draws on Leah Mermelstein's coaching steps and Jocelyn Seamer's balanced advice. The conclusion is that teachers should prioritise efficiency along with effectiveness while keeping rigor.
points: Short complete works like Of Mice and Men or plays can keep rigor while fitting limited classroom time, so page count alone is not the issue.
Plays are written to be seen and heard, and reading them aloud makes participation natural.
Social studies time is a simpler lever for reading gains than adding knowledge-building ELA content that is not aligned to it.
Reading instruction has swung through burn-the-bridge overcorrections, such as overteaching phonics and revising programs, which breeds cynicism.
Adopt practices by asking whether they improve learning enough to justify their implementation costs, and coach through purpose, success criteria, action and early measurement.
quotes: I’m merely suggesting that we might be missing the whole forest of literature because we’re fixating on certain types of trees.

I never understood this stance since a play is written to be viewed, not read. The Greek classics were all performed—as, of course, were Shakespeare’s plays—long before the first English novel, Robinson Crusoe, appeared in the early 1700’s.

We are right to be concerned about the state of our instructional methods and materials—and how students respond to each—but we are wrong to think that page count alone will make a big difference without other meaningful changes to our lessons.
In fact, social studies is the only subject with a clear, positive, and statistically significant effect on reading improvement.
This revolving door of methods and materials is what invites cynicism about our profession to set in and fester.
I freely admit that if I can find a way to make my teaching life easier without sacrificing the success of my students, I’ll take it every single time.

This question, Does X improve learning enough to justify its implementation costs compared to alternative Y? is the one that can prevent us from crossing all those bridges to nowhere, a question we should be asking anytime we are presented with a research-based strategy to adopt.
